meaning: A changing mix of many bright colours or things; also a toy tube with coloured patterns
trick: KALEIDOSCOPE: a scope full of colourful 'kaleido' (beautiful) shapes.
examples: On either side of them is a kaleidoscope of wildflowers swaying in the wind.
The market was a kaleidoscope of colours and sounds.

meaning: Liking someone or something a lot; also eager
trick: KEEN on someone = KEEN to be near them.
examples: I was rather keen on her in those days, and I think she liked me too.
My son is very keen on football.

usage.pattern: be keen on someone/something / keen to do something

meaning: A person who looks after a place, building or animals; also a goalkeeper
trick: KEEPER = the one who KEEPS (looks after) the place.
examples: The keeper switched on the lamps, and I was almost blinded by the light.
The zoo keeper fed the lions at noon.

usage.pattern: the keeper of something / zoo/park keeper

meaning: A thin fuel oil used in stoves and lamps (US; British 'paraffin')
trick: KEROSENE = the oil in the 'kero' (kerosene) stove and lamp.
examples: The kitchen had pots and pans, a pressure cooker and a kerosene stove.
When the power went off, we lit the kerosene lamp.

meaning: Main or most important, especially the chief talk at a big event
trick: KEY + NOTE: the KEY speech everyone takes NOTE of.
examples: He'd talk about some charity event where he was supposed to be the keynote speaker.
The company's boss gave the keynote speech at the conference.

meaning: To light a fire; also to make a feeling start
trick: KINDLE = KIND of a little flame to start a fire.
examples: Nana showed her how to knead dough and how to kindle the tandoor.
We used dry leaves to kindle the campfire.

usage.pattern: kindle a fire / kindle someone's interest

meaning: Small dry sticks and twigs used to start a fire
hindi: आग जलाने की लकड़ियाँ, सूखी टहनियाँ
trick: KINDLING is what you use to KINDLE a fire.
examples: Think of your small accomplishments as kindling.
We gathered kindling before lighting the campfire.

usage.pattern: use something as kindling / gather kindling

meaning: A feeling of being close to someone; also family relationship
trick: KIN = family; KINSHIP = feeling like family.
examples: She felt for the first time a kinship with her husband.
The two players felt a kinship because they came from the same town.

meaning: A small open stall or booth that sells things like snacks, toys or newspapers
trick: KIOSK: a tiny shop where you can 'Kiss-an-ASK' for a quick item.
examples: From a toy kiosk, Zalmai picked out a rubber basketball.
I bought a newspaper from the kiosk at the station.

usage.pattern: a + something + kiosk / buy from a kiosk

meaning: Given or wearing all the clothes and equipment needed (often followed by up/out; mainly British)
trick: KITTED = got your whole KIT on.
examples: The class was divided into groups of five and fully kitted up.
The players were kitted out in new uniforms.

usage.pattern: be kitted up / kitted out (in/with something)

meaning: A special skill or talent for doing something well, often naturally
trick: KNACK = KNOW + HACK: knowing the trick of it.
examples: Hosseini has that rare thing, a knack for storytelling.
She has a knack for making people laugh.

meaning: A person who buys old or worn-out horses and kills them for meat or other uses (British, old-fashioned)
trick: A KNACKERed (worn-out) horse goes to the KNACKER.
examples: When your strength goes, Jones will sell you to the knacker.
The farmer sold the old, tired horse to the knacker.

meaning: To press and fold dough firmly with your hands
trick: KNEAD the dough because you NEED bread (silent K).
examples: Nana showed her how to knead dough.
Knead the flour and water for ten minutes.

meaning: Pressing and folding dough firmly with the hands
trick: KNEADING = the silent-K way of making dough you NEED.
examples: She made fresh dough, kneading it the way Nana had shown her.
My mother was kneading dough for rotis.

meaning: Made by joining wool or thread in loops with long needles; also joined closely together
trick: KNIT with a silent K: the K is the needle knitting.
examples: The bed had a green-flowered blanket knit in a honeycomb design.
My grandma knit me a warm sweater.

meaning: Making clothes from wool using long needles
trick: KNITTING: needles 'nit-nit' clicking.
examples: By the way her arms moved, I guessed that she was knitting.
My aunt sits by the window, knitting a scarf.

meaning: A round handle on a door or drawer; also a round button to control a machine
trick: KNOB: a round NOB-shaped handle you turn.
examples: Laila turned the knob and walked in.
Turn the knob to change the volume.

meaning: Small round lumps, such as the bones down the back of the neck; also round handles
trick: KNOBS = little round bumps, like door knobs on your spine.
examples: His thick fingers slowly pressed the knobs in the back of her neck.
The cupboard has small brass knobs.

meaning: A small round hill
trick: KNOLL: a hill that ROLLs gently up.
examples: There was a small knoll which was the highest point on the farm.
We had a picnic on a grassy knoll.

meaning: Small groups of people or things close together; also tied loops in rope
trick: KNOTS of villages, tied together like knots in a rope.
examples: They passed small towns, big towns and knots of little villages.
Knots of students stood chatting outside the hall.

meaning: A joint of a finger, especially where it joins the hand
trick: KNUCKLE: you knock on a door with your knuckles.
examples: She sucked air through her teeth and bit on the knuckle of her thumb.
He cracked his knuckles before typing.

meaning: A person's one great weakness (informal; from Superman's weakness)
trick: KRYPTONITE is the only thing that weakens SUPERMAN.
examples: The pool had been my kryptonite.
Chocolate is my kryptonite when I'm dieting.
